doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Staying close to the studios, no tours and no pagers
summary: He mostly just recorded, lived near the studios in Studio City, and explains last-minute calls from pay phones.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: If you had an offer to do like a three week tour with some fantastic band that was put together to do a tour of the country, would that have been hard for you, like you’re taking yourself out of the scene and you’re not making the dates people want?
Are you talking about back in the day or now?

Yeah I really didn’t do much of that. I would just record for them and then they would get bands and musicians to take on the road. You know I just did the records. I really didn’t, I was so busy I was enjoying going home for lunch, you know I lived in Studio City and I’d be at Universal and I’d come home for lunch and Seely would have lunch with me. Or dinner. I lived close. I always wanted to be close. And I would tell musicians too that first moved to town, I said if you want to be close, you need to be close because © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

you get a last minute call, somebody can’t make it or their car broke down or they got — whatever, something happened, and we need somebody right away, you get a phone call and we need you right away you know. Can you get there in like 20 minutes or something like that. And so back in those days you could. If you lived in North Hollywood, Studio City, anywhere like that, everything was in Hollywood pretty much or Burbank. Pretty much Hollywood, the studios are in Hollywood. And they could be there in 15 minutes, 20 minutes.
Well pre-cell phone, did you have beepers or something?

No. We didn’t have anything. This was before pagers or any of that. It was just go to the pay phone or use the studio phone and call them and say can you get here right away. And they’d come as fast as they could. Oh no, those are times when we were concerned — when somebody was late we were concerned about the fact that maybe they were in an accident or they got sick. That was our concern. It wasn’t — it had nothing to do with the business like somebody running over on a session. You know that happened all the time. Say somebody’s ten minutes late, okay we’ll start with the ten. Because they’re in traffic. And there was no panic, everything was fine, you know it was relaxed. And we would always get it done and with smiles on their faces and our faces too. As we’d leave and go do another session. So it was all good, Monk.
